Reed-Solomon codes achieve list decoding capacity. In this section, we prove this conjecture. The proof follows from some of the results we use to prove Theorem 1.5. We first introduce the necessary notation to properly state Conjecture 5.7 of [ST20].
Let C be a [n,k]-code with generator matrix G. Let J1,…,Jt⊆[n]. We define a block matrix MG,(J1,…,Jt) with (t2)​k columns and (t−12)​k+∑i≠j|Ji∩Jj| rows as follows.
To describe the entries of M, we split the columns of M into (t2) blocks of size k, where we identify each block with a pair {i,j}∈([t]2). For the rows, we have two types (a) and (b), which consist of (t−12)​k and ∑i≠j|Ji∩Jj| rows, respectively. For the (a)-type rows, we split them into (t−12) blocks of size k, where identify the blocks with pairs {i,j}∈([t−1]2). For the (b)-type rows, we split them into (t2) blocks, which are identified with pairs {i,j}∈([t]2). The (i,j)th type-(b) row block has |Ji∩Jj rows. The entries of M are filled in as follows.
(a) 
Consider the type (a) row block indexed by {i,j}∈([t−1]2) with i<j. Where this row meets the column blocks {i,j} and {j,t}, we insert the identity matrix Ik. Where this row meets the column block {i,t}, the matrix −Ik appears. All other entries in this row block are zero.
(b) 
Consider the type (b) row block indexed by {i,j}⊆[t]. Where this row block meets column block {i,j}, we insert the matrix G⊤|Ji∩Jj. All other entries in this row block are zero.
The following lemma of [ST20] relates MG,(J1,…,Jt) to list decoding properties of C.
4.8[ST20], lightly edited.
Let t⩾2 and τ⩾1. Assume there exists c1,c2,…,ct∈C∩Bτ​(y). Then, there exist J1,…,Jt such that |Ji|⩾n−τ for all i and MG,(J1,…,Jt) does not have full column rank.
To give intuition about M, we include an adaptation of [ST20]’s proof of this lemma for completeness.
Proof.
For all i∈[t], let Ji be the set of coordinates for which ci and y are equal. Since ci∈Bτ​(y), we have that |Ji|⩾n−τ. Since G is the generator matrix of C, for all i∈[t], there exists a unique fi∈𝔽k such that ci=G⊤​fi. For all i,j∈[t] with i<j let fi​j=fj−fi.
Let v be a column vector of length (t2)​k which is the fi​j’s concatenated together in the same order as the column blocks {i,j}∈([t]2) of M. To complete the proof, it suffices to show that v≠0 but M​v=0.
First, to see why v≠0, note that
G⊤​f01=G⊤​(f1−f0)=c1−c0≠0.
Thus, f01≠0, so v≠0.
Second, to see why M​v=0, we split the analysis into the type (a) rows and the type (b) rows. For the type (a) rows, for each i<j∈[t] note that M​v restricted to this row block equals fi​j+fj​t−fi​t=(fj−fi)+(ft−fj)−(ft−fi)=0. For the type (b) rows, it suffices to check for all i<j∈[t] that G⊤|Ji∩Jj​fi​j=0. Observe that
G⊤|Ji∩Jj​fi​j=G⊤|Ji∩Jj​(fj−fi)=(cj−ci)|Ji∩Jj
Note that, by definition, for all indices a∈Ji∩Jj, we have that (cj)a=ya=(ci)a. Thus, the above expression does indeed equal zero. Therefore, M​v=0.
Thus, M lacks full column rank.
∎
As a result of this lemma, [ST20] formulated the following conjecture whose resolution also implies that generic Reed-Solomon codes reach list-decoding capacity.
4.9Conjecture 5.7 of [ST20]–restated.
Let J1,…,Jt⊆[n] be such that for all S⊆[t],

and further that (19) is an equality when S=[t]. Let G be a generic [n,k]-Vandermonde matrix. Then, MG,(J1,…,Jt) has full column rank.
We now prove this conjecture.
Proof.
Note that MG,(J1,…,Jt) only includes entries from the ith column of G if i∈Jj for some j∈[t]. In particular, MG,(J1,…,Jt) has full column rank if and only if MG|J1∪⋯∪Jt,(J1,…,Jt) has full column rank. Thus, we may assume without loss off generality that G=G|J1∪⋯∪Jt. In other words,
⋃i∈[t]Ji=[n].

Also observe that for any i∈[t], if we look at (19) with S=[t]∖{i} and subtract from it the equality case of (19) with S=[t], we get that

Since |⋃j∈[t]Jj|−|⋃j∈[t]∖{i}Jj|⩾0, we have that

Assume for sake of contradiction that MG,(J1,…,Jt) lacks full column rank. Thus, there exists nonzero v∈𝔽(t2)​k such that M​v=0. For each i<j∈[n], let fi​j∈𝔽k be the block of v corresponding to (i,j). Further, define ft=0 and fi=−fi​t for all i∈[t−1]. We claim that for all i<j∈[n] that fi​j=fj−fi. This is by definition when j=t. Otherwise, if j<t, then by the type (a) rows of M, we may deduce that fi​j−fi​t+fj​t=0, which implies that fi​j=fj−fi.
For all i∈[t], define ci=G⊤​fi. Since v≠0, we know that fi​j≠0 for some i<j. Thus, for some i<j, we have that ci≠cj.
Due to the type (b) rows of M, we can deduce for all i<j∈[n] that G⊤|Ji∩Jj​fi​j=0, so G⊤|Ji∩Jj​fi=G⊤|Ji∩Jj​fj. Therefore, ci|Ji∩Jj=cj|Ji∩Jj.
Let y∈𝔽n be a vector such that yJi=(ci)|Ji for all i. Note that at least one y must exist because each of the ci’s are consistent.
For all i∈[t], let J¯i=[n]∖Ji and ui=ci−y. Note that supp⁡(ui)⊆J¯i. Let H be the parity-check matrix of C. Then, since H​c1=⋯=H​ct, we have that Hu1=⋯Hut. Thus, the vector (−u1,u2,u3,…,uL) is in the kernel of the following matrix.

Since the ci’s are not all equal, the ui’s are not all 0. Therefore, by Proposition 4.6, we have that

By (21), so |J¯i|⩽n−k for all i∈[t]. Since H is MDS, we therefore have that dim(H|J¯i)=|J¯i| for all i∈[t]. Thus, we can deduce that HJ¯1∩⋯∩HJ¯t≠0.

5 Computing Generic Intersection Dimension in Polynomial Time
In this section, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for computing the generic intersection dimension of a family of sets. Let A1,…,Aℓ⊆[n] be sets of size at most k. Consider the following linear program:
Primal LP
minimize:
k−∑i=1ℓδi
subject to:
∀i∈[ℓ],
δi
⩾0
∀I⊆[ℓ]​(I≠∅),
∑i∈Iδi
⩽k−|AI|.
By Theorem 1.16 and Lemma 2.8, we know that the optimal integral solution to this linear program is equal to the generic intersection dimension of A1,…,Aℓ. In fact, we shall prove that the optimal “fractional” has the same objective value.
5.1.
The objective value of the Primal LP is equal to the k-dimensional generic intersection dimension of A1,…,Aℓ.
